title: The Aliasing Trap
concept: When two variables point to the same mutable object, changes through one affect the other!

content.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a  # NOT a copy!

print(f"a = {a}")
print(f"b = {b}")
print(f"Same object? {a is b}")

b[0] = 999

print(f"After b[0] = 999:")
print(f"a = {a}")  # SURPRISE!
print(f"b = {b}")

steps.title: Create a list
steps.explanation:
Create a list and bind `a` to it.

So far, one object, one name.

steps.title: b = a - THE TRAP!
steps.explanation:
**THIS IS NOT A COPY!**

`b = a` makes `b` point to the SAME object as `a`.

Now we have:
- Two names: `a` and `b`
- ONE object: `[1, 2, 3]`

This is called **aliasing** - two names for the same object.

steps.title: a is b → True!
steps.explanation:
**PROOF:** `a is b` returns `True`!

This confirms they point to the EXACT SAME object.

Not just equal values, but the same memory location.

steps.title: Modify through b...
steps.explanation:
`b[0] = 999` modifies the list object.

Since `a` and `b` both point to the SAME object...

**What will `a` show?**

steps.title: a ALSO changed!
steps.explanation:
**THE SURPRISE:**

We modified through `b`, but `a` also shows the change!

**Why?** Because there's only ONE list. Both names point to it.

**This is the #1 source of bugs for Python beginners.**

quiz.question:
What prints?

x = [1, 2]
y = x
y = y + [3]
print(x)
quiz.explanation: y = y + [3] creates a NEW list and rebinds y to it. This BREAKS the alias! x still points to [1, 2]. If we had used y.append(3) or y += [3], x would see the change.

misconceptions.wrong: b = a creates a copy of the list
misconceptions.correct: b = a makes b point to the same list as a
misconceptions.why: Assignment binds names to objects. It never copies objects.

misconceptions.wrong: Each variable has its own independent list
misconceptions.correct: Multiple variables can share the same list object
misconceptions.why: This aliasing is a feature, not a bug - but it can cause unexpected mutations.

misconceptions.wrong: Only b changed, a should be the same
misconceptions.correct: There's only ONE list - both names see the change
misconceptions.why: The object is shared. Mutation through any name affects all names.

keyTakeaway: b = a creates an ALIAS, not a copy! Changes through b affect a because they're the SAME object!
